original: Take 5g a day as a baseline. The point of that baseline is to counter the breakdown of the gut lining that high-intensity or high-volume training causes, like CrossFit or intense cardio. If your immune system is dealing with an acute exposure, if your whole system is under a lot of stress, or if you have active IBD (Crohn's or colitis), raise it gradually to 10-30g a day.
rewrite: Take 5g a day as a baseline, to keep your enterocytes fed. The 5g also counters the breakdown of the gut lining that hard or long training causes, like CrossFit or intense cardio. While you train, your body sends blood away from your gut to your working muscles, so your enterocytes get less oxygen and fuel. But the glutamine you swallow doesn't need that blood, since it reaches them from inside your gut. If your immune system is dealing with an acute exposure, if your whole system is under a lot of stress, or if you have active IBD (Crohn's or colitis), raise it gradually to 10-30g a day.

I thought exercise was good for the body"; "the blood carries them?"): strenuous exercise redistributes blood to the working muscles and skin, which significantly reduces blood flow to the gut, leading to hypoperfusion and loss of epithelial integrity (van Wijck 2012, abstract: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22517770/); high-intensity or prolonged exercise diverts blood from the gut to the muscles, and the ischemia raises intestinal permeability, while moderate exercise like walking and yoga helps the barrier (systematic review, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12175863/). "Starving" ties it to the section's first paragraph (energy starvation: without energy, the barrier loosens). Check that this is true and not overstated The last sentence is the paragraph before's own point ("your enterocytes can take it in as soon as it reaches them"): two readers asked how swallowed glutamine could make up for what the blood no longer brings. Check it doesn't claim the glutamine replaces the oxygen
